title: Top 10 Everyday Verbs and More Precise Alternatives
dek: Learn when get, make, do, go, say and think are enough, and when a more precise verb says it better, with examples, grammar notes and practice.

blocks.text: What you will learn
By the end of this guide you will be able to choose a more precise verb when your meaning is specific, and to recognise when the simple verb is already the best choice.

Verbs such as **get, make, do, have, go, say, think, look, know** and **give** are not mistakes. They are among the most flexible words in English, and native speakers use them all day. The aim is not to replace them. It is to add precise options for the moments when *get* or *make* is too vague for what you mean.
Three rules before you start

items: **Decide the meaning first.** *Get* can mean receive, earn, understand or arrive. Each meaning has a different, more precise verb.
**Check the grammar.** A new verb often needs a different pattern: *tell* needs a person (*told me*), *notice* takes no preposition, *arrive* takes *at* or *in*.
**Ask whether the simple verb is better.** If the precise verb sounds heavy or formal for the situation, keep the simple one.

blocks.text: The 10 verbs, organised by meaning

The tables show a common meaning of the everyday verb, a more precise option, and an example. The notes mark formal or regional uses. These are not universal synonyms: each option fits only the meaning shown.
1. Get

rows: get an email or a parcel
I received your email yesterday. (neutral to formal; "I got your email" is also natural)
You must obtain a visa before you travel.
My English has improved a lot this year.
We reached the hotel at noon. / We arrived in Lyon at noon.
I collect my daughter from school at four.
blocks.caption: Get: choose by meaning

blocks.text: **Watch out:** *get + adjective* (*get tired, get angry, get cold*) is perfectly natural: *I get tired after long meetings.* *Become* is possible but sounds more formal, or describes a lasting change: *She became a doctor.*
2. Make

rows: The factory produces 500 cars a day.
She designed a new logo for the café.
They built a new bridge over the river.
He earns a good living as a translator.
They set up their company in 2019.
blocks.caption: Make: choose by meaning

blocks.text: **Watch out:** many *make* phrases are fixed and should not be replaced: *make a decision, make a mistake, make progress, make an effort.*
3. Do

rows: The team carried out a survey of 200 students.
I completed the exercise before class.
I am taking my English exam in June.
blocks.caption: Do: choose by meaning

blocks.text: **Watch out:** *do the dishes, do your best, do business* and *do the shopping* are fixed. *Do* is the right verb there.
4. Have

rows: We hold a team meeting every Monday.
have a car or a flat
She owns two flats in Lyon.
blocks.caption: Have: choose by meaning

blocks.text: **Watch out:** *I have a car* is the natural way to say it. *I possess a car* sounds odd in conversation.
5. Go

rows: go to a conference or class
go to live in another country
He relocated to Canada for work.
We visited the castle on Sunday.
We are heading to the station.
blocks.caption: Go: choose by meaning

blocks.text: **Watch out:** *go home, go shopping, go for a walk* are natural as they are.
6. Say

rows: She told me that she was late.
He mentioned the deadline in passing.
The teacher explained the rule to us.
The company announced a new policy.
say it is true without proof
He claims that he never received the email.
She admitted that she had made a mistake.
I suggest that we start earlier.
blocks.caption: Say: choose by meaning

blocks.text: **Grammar point:** you *say* something, but you *tell* someone. Say: *She told me she was late*. Not: *She said me she was late.*
7. Think

rows: I believe this is the right decision.
I assume the train is on time.
I suspect he forgot the meeting.
I expect it will rain tomorrow.
We are considering a different supplier.
blocks.caption: Think: choose by meaning

blocks.text: **Watch out:** *I think* is natural and very common. Swapping it for *in my estimation* in conversation sounds stiff. Use the other verbs when they add meaning (doubt, strong belief, no proof), not to sound advanced.
8. Look

rows: He stared at the screen. / We gazed at the sea.
I noticed a mistake on page two.
blocks.caption: Look: choose by meaning

blocks.text: **Watch out:** *stare* can feel rude; *gaze* is calmer, often admiring. Patterns: *look at*, *glance at*, *stare at*, but *watch* and *notice* take no preposition.
9. Know
These are not synonyms of *know*. They describe different moments or kinds of knowing, which is why they are useful.

rows: know someone you have seen before
I realised I had left my keys at home.
I understand how the system works.
Are you aware of the new rules?
I am familiar with this software.
She mastered the technique after two years.
blocks.caption: Know: choose by meaning

blocks.text: **Watch out:** *I know the answer* needs no upgrade.
10. Give

rows: The jury awarded first prize to a young poet.
blocks.caption: Give: choose by meaning

blocks.text: **Grammar point:** *provide someone with something* (*provide us with training*) or *provide something for someone*. *Give me a hand* is an idiom; keep it.
Three more everyday verbs

rows: Leave the files on the desk.
blocks.caption: Like, use and put

blocks.text: **Watch out:** *use* is usually the best word, and *utilise* rarely adds anything. Do not turn *I like reading* into *I am passionate about reading* unless you really mean it: the meaning changes.
Formal writing: a few useful upgrades
In reports and academic writing, some everyday verbs have more precise choices. In speech with friends, the simple verb is usually better.

rows: The study demonstrates a steady increase.
The team resolved the issue within an hour.
The company launched a new product in May.
Engineers identified the cause of the delay.
blocks.caption: Formal register

blocks.text: When the simple verb is the right choice

items: *I got home late.* Natural as it is.
*Could you give me a hand?* A fixed idiom.
*I will make some coffee.* *Produce coffee* would sound strange.
*We use this app every day.* *Use* is the best word.
*I think it is a good idea.* Natural and clear.

blocks.text: **Rule of thumb:** before you swap a verb, ask three questions.

items: Does the new verb keep my meaning?
Does it work with the same grammar (preposition, object)?
Would I say or write this in this situation?

blocks.text: Collocations differ between languages

In English you *make* a decision. French says *prendre une décision* (literally "take"), Russian says *принять решение* ("accept/take"), and Greek says *παίρνω απόφαση* ("take"). Translating word for word causes errors, so learn verb + noun chunks, not single verbs.
Practice: choose the best verb

blocks.question: She ___ a lot of money from her online shop.
blocks.explanation: *Earn* is the verb for money you get from work. *Made* would also be natural here, but it is not an option.

blocks.question: You need to ___ a visa before you travel.
blocks.explanation: *Obtain* fits formal, official contexts. *Get a visa* is also fine in speech.

blocks.question: The manager ___ us that the meeting was cancelled.
blocks.explanation: *Tell* needs a person after it (*told us*). *Said us* and *mentioned us that* are not correct.

blocks.question: She ___ quickly at her watch and left.
blocks.explanation: *Glance* means a quick look. *Stare* means a long look, so it does not fit with *quickly*.

blocks.question: I did not ___ the mistake until I read the email again.
blocks.explanation: *Notice* means to see something and become aware of it. The other verbs describe how you look, not the moment you become aware.

blocks.question: We ___ this app every day to book rooms.
blocks.explanation: *Use* is the natural everyday word. *Utilise* is unnecessarily formal, and *operate* is for machines.

blocks.text: Now use it

items: **Rewrite:** take five sentences from your own emails or messages that contain *get, make, do, have* or *go*. Change a verb only where it makes the meaning clearer, and leave the others alone.
**Speak:** record a one-minute message about your last holiday or week at work. Use at least three verbs from this guide.
**Review tomorrow:** without looking, write the more precise verb for *get a visa*, *go to a conference*, *give a speech* and *know someone's voice*. Check yourself against the tables.

blocks.text: Next steps

Continue with [Stop Saying "Very": 50 Stronger Words](replace-very-50-stronger-adjectives.html) and [Replace 50 Overused Phrases](replace-50-overused-phrases.html). Together the three articles cover verbs, adjectives and phrases.
Final thought: precision, not replacement
Good English is not the most complicated English. It is English where each word does its job. Keep *get* and *make* for everyday life. Reach for a precise verb when you need one.
